claims.claim: Most miR-30-based shRNAs did not efficiently silence Venus expression.
claims.source: To determine their knockdown efficiency, we induced their expression in cells carrying sensor plasmids in which the fluorophore Venus was linked to either the CD95L or CD95 open reading frame (ORF). Expression of most of these miR-30-based shRNAs also did not efficiently silence Venus expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: shL3 and shR6 expressed in the Tet-inducible pTIP vector killed HeyA8 cells and efficiently suppressed Venus fluorescence.
claims.source: In contrast, two of our most toxic shRNAs shL3 and shR6 when expressed in the Tet-inducible pTIP vector not only killed HeyA8 cells, but also very efficiently suppressed Venus fluorescence in cells expressing the targeted Venus sensor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: The levels of shRNAs produced from the miR-30-based vector may not be sufficient to be toxic to cancer cells.
claims.source: These data suggest that the levels of shRNAs produced from the miR-30-based vector may not be sufficient to be toxic to the cancer cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of toxicity and knockdown efficiency of miR-30-based shRNAs.

claims.claim: Growth of HeyA8 cells was effectively blocked when siL3 was transfected at 1 nM.
claims.source: Growth was effectively blocked (and cells died, data not shown) when siL3 was transfected at 1 nM—a concentration well below the commonly used and recommended siRNA concentration of 5–50 nM)—but not at 0.1 nM.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: Exogenously added recombinant CD95L protein did not protect NB7 cells from the toxicity of CD95L-derived shRNAs.
claims.source: When NB7 cells were incubated with different concentrations of a soluble form of CD95L (S2), toxicity exerted by shL1 was not affected (Figure 1A, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: NB7 neuroblastoma cells lack expression of caspase-8 and are completely resistant to the apoptosis-inducing effects of CD95L.
claims.source: NB7 neuroblastoma cells were chosen for these experiments because they lack expression of caspase-8 (Teitz et al., 2000) and hence are completely resistant to the apoptosis-inducing effects of CD95L.
claims.evidence: This is based on published literature (Teitz et al., 2000).

claims.claim: Overexpression of shRNA-resistant versions of the CD95L ORF did not protect NB7 cells from shL1 or shL3.
claims.source: Overexpression of these shRNA-resistant versions of the CD95L ORF did not protect the cells from shL1 or shL3, respectively (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Expression of wild-type or mutated CD95 in MCF-7 cells did not reduce the toxicity of shR6 or shR7.
claims.source: Neither expression of wild-type (wt) nor mutated (MUT) CD95 in MCF-7 cells (Figure 1F) reduced the toxicity when cells were infected with the pLKO-shR6 or another toxic lentiviral shRNA, pLKO-shR7 (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claims.claim: Neither exogenously added recombinant CD95L nor exogenously expressed CD95L or CD95 protein can protect cells from toxic shRNAs derived from these genes.
claims.source: These data suggested that neither exogenously added recombinant CD95L or exogenously expressed CD95L or CD95 protein can protect cells from toxic shRNAs derived from these genes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing lack of protection by CD95L or CD95 protein.

claims.claim: A 41 nt piece of the CD95L gene containing the target site for shL3 was deleted in 293T cells using CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing.
claims.source: We first deleted a 41 nt piece of the CD95L gene in 293T cells, that contained the target site for shL3 (Figure 2A and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claims.claim: 293T shL3 Δ41 cells were equally sensitive to the toxic shRNA shL3 compared to control cells.
claims.source: Compared to a pool of control cells transfected only with the Cas9 plasmid, the 293T shL3 Δ41 cells were equally sensitive to the toxic shRNA (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: HeyA8 cells with homozygous deletion of the shR6 site were still fully toxic to shR6.
claims.source: In all cases, the shRNA or siRNA that targeted the deleted region was still fully toxic to the target-site deleted cells (Figure 2H and I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: HeyA8 cells with homozygous deletion of the siL3 site were still fully toxic to siL3.
claims.source: In all cases, the shRNA or siRNA that targeted the deleted region was still fully toxic to the target-site deleted cells (Figure 2H and I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: Efficient growth reduction and cell death were observed in siL3 site-deleted cells transfected with as little as 1 nM siL3.
claims.source: We saw efficient growth reduction and cell death in siL3 site-deleted cells transfected with as little as 1 nM siL3 (Figure 2I, and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: Cells were not dying due to the knockdown of either CD95 or CD95L.
claims.source: These data firmly establish that cells were not dying due to the knockdown of either CD95 or CD95L.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing toxicity in cells with deleted target sites.

claims.claim: Double-stranded siL3 effectively silenced Venus expression and induced toxicity.
claims.source: While double-stranded (ds)-siL3 effectively silenced Venus expression and induced toxicity, neither the sense nor the antisense single-stranded (ss)RNAs significantly decreased Venus expression or induced toxicity (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Single-stranded sense or antisense siL3 RNAs did not significantly decrease Venus expression or induce toxicity.
claims.source: While double-stranded (ds)-siL3 effectively silenced Venus expression and induced toxicity, neither the sense nor the antisense single-stranded (ss)RNAs significantly decreased Venus expression or induced toxicity (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: No activity was found when ds-siL3, synthesized as deoxyribo-oligonucleotides, was transfected into cells.
claims.source: In addition, no activity was found when ds-siL3, synthesized as deoxyribo-oligonucleotides, was transfected into the cells (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Converting siL3 to a blunt-end duplex resulted in substantial loss of RNAi activity and toxicity.
claims.source: Converting siL3 to a blunt-end duplex resulted in substantial loss of RNAi activity and toxicity (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: A 5' modification in the guide strand of siL3 prevented RNAi activity and toxicity.
claims.source: Only when the siL3 duplex carried a 5' modification in the guide strand did it prevent RNAi activity and toxicity; modifications in the three other positions had no effect (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: siL3MUT reduced the growth inhibitory activity of siL3 in a dose-dependent fashion.
claims.source: siL3MUT reduced the growth inhibitory activity of siL3 in a dose-dependent fashion suggesting that siL3 and siL3MUT compete for the same binding site in the cells, pointing at involvement of the RISC.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: siL3 and siL3MUT compete for the same binding site in cells, pointing at involvement of the RISC.
claims.source: siL3MUT reduced the growth inhibitory activity of siL3 in a dose-dependent fashion suggesting that siL3 and siL3MUT compete for the same binding site in the cells, pointing at involvement of the RISC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the competition experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Dicer-/- cells were completely resistant to the toxic effects of shL3 or shR6.
claims.source: Consistent with the requirement of Dicer to process shRNAs, Dicer-/- cells were completely resistant to the toxic shRNAs (Figure 3E, center panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: shR6 could not silence CD95 protein expression in Dicer-/- cells.
claims.source: This was also supported by the inability of shR6 to silence CD95 protein expression in these cells (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Dicer-/- cells died when transfected with siL3.
claims.source: Dicer-/- cells were not resistant to toxic siRNAs as these cells died when transfected with siL3, which is consistent with mature siRNAs not needing further processing by Dicer (Figure 3G, center panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Drosha-/- cells were hypersensitive to the two toxic shRNAs shL3 and shR6.
claims.source: Interestingly, Drosha-/- cells were hypersensitive to the two toxic shRNAs (Figure 3E, right panel, p<0.0001, according to a polynomial fitting model)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: shR6 efficiently knocked down CD95 expression in Drosha-/- cells.
claims.source: and shR6 efficiently knocked down CD95 expression in Drosha-/- cells (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Both Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells were much more susceptible to the toxicity induced by siL3 than parental cells.
claims.source: Both Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells were much more susceptible to the toxicity induced by siL3 than parental cells (Figure 3G, center and right panel, p<0.0001, according to a polynomial fitting model).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The hypersensitivity of Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells to toxic si/shRNAs is explained by more efficient uptake of mature toxic RNAi-active species into the RISC because they are almost completely devoid of competing endogenous miRNAs.
claims.source: The hypersensitivity of the Drosha-/- cells to toxic si/shRNAs and of Dicer-/- cells to toxic siRNAs can be explained by Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells allowing much more efficient uptake of mature toxic RNAi-active species into the RISC because they are almost completely devoid of competing endogenous miRNAs (Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the hypersensitivity data and knowledge about miRNA depletion in these cells (Kim et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The 6mer seed sequence of siL3 was critical for both RNAi activity and its toxicity.
claims.source: These data suggest the 6mer seed sequence of siL3 was critical for both RNAi activity and its toxicity.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the chimeric siRNA experiments shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: One mRNA was upregulated and 11 mRNAs were downregulated in cells treated with toxic shL3 and shR6.
claims.source: The combination of the analyses resulted in one mRNA that was upregulated and 11 mRNAs that were downregulated (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: For nine of the eleven downregulated genes, published data suggest they are either highly upregulated in cancer and/or critical for the survival of cancer cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, for nine of the eleven genes, published data suggest they are either highly upregulated in cancer and/or critical for the survival of cancer cells, as their inhibition or knockdown resulted in either growth reduction or induction of various forms of cell death (see legend of Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for details).
claims.evidence: This is based on published literature cited in the legend of Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Six of the eleven downregulated genes were identified in two independent genome-wide lethality screens to be critical for cancer cell survival.
claims.source: Significantly, six of these eleven downregulated genes were recently identified in two independent genome-wide lethality screens to be critical for cancer cell survival (Blomen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on published genome-wide screens (Blomen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).

claims.claim: There was a significant enrichment (54.5%, p-value=3×10−6) of survival genes among the genes downregulated during DISE.
claims.source: Considering these two screens only identified 6.6% of human genes to be critical for cell survival, we found a significant enrichment (54.5%, p-value=3×10−6 according to binomial distribution) of these survival genes among the genes downregulated during the cell death induced by either shL3 or shR6.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the RNA-Seq data compared to published survival gene lists.

claims.claim: All six survival genes downregulated during DISE are either highly amplified or mutated in human cancers.
claims.source: All six survival genes are either highly amplified or mutated in human cancers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Most of the deregulated mRNAs were downregulated early with a significant effect already at 14 hr, more than two days before the onset of cell death.
claims.source: A kinetic analysis showed most of the deregulated mRNAs were downregulated early with a significant effect already at 14 hr, more than two days before the onset of cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by kinetic qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Cells were dying because of the silencing of multiple critical survival genes.
claims.source: This suggested the cells were dying because of the silencing of multiple critical survival genes, providing an explanation for why multiple cell death pathways were activated.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-Seq data showing downregulation of multiple survival genes.

claims.claim: Individual knockdown of seven of the eleven downregulated genes resulted in reduced cell growth in HeyA8 cells.
claims.source: Individual knockdown of seven of the targeted genes resulted in reduced cell growth when compared to cells transfected with a pool of scrambled siRNAs (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: 1 nM of a mixture of siRNA pools targeting seven survival genes was sufficient to effectively reduce growth of HeyA8 cells.
claims.source: Remarkably, 1 nM of this siRNA mixture (35.7 pM of each individual siRNA) was sufficient to effectively reduce growth of the cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) and also cause substantial cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: Survival genes were significantly enriched towards the top of the ranked lists (most downregulated) in all four RNA-Seq data sets.
claims.source: In all cases, survival genes were significantly enriched towards the top of the ranked lists (most downregulated). In contrast, nonsurvival genes were not enriched.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Of the 16 genes that were significantly downregulated in cells treated with any of the four sh/siRNAs, 12 were histones.
claims.source: One interesting feature of DISE that emerged was the substantial loss of histones. Of the 16 genes that were significantly downregulated in cells treated with any of the four sh/siRNAs, 12 were histones (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Losing histones is a specific aspect of DISE because the downregulated histones were not the most highly expressed genes in these cells.
claims.source: While it might be expected that dying cells would downregulate highly expressed genes such as histones, we believe that losing histones is a specific aspect of DISE because a detailed analysis revealed the downregulated histones were not the most highly expressed genes in these cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Genes involved in mitotic cell cycle, DNA conformation change, and macromolecular complex assembly were among the most significantly downregulated across all cells in which DISE was induced.
claims.source: A Metascape analysis revealed genes involved in mitotic cell cycle, DNA conformation change, and macromolecular complex assembly were among the most significantly downregulated across all cells in which DISE was induced by any of the four sh/siRNAs (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Metascape analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Sylamer analysis identified a strong enrichment of the cognate seed match for shL3 and shR6 in cells treated with either of these two shRNAs.
claims.source: This analysis identified a strong enrichment of the cognate seed match for shL3 and shR6 in cells treated with either of these two shRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Sylamer analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Enrichment in 6mers and 8mers were both detected in the 3'UTRs but not the ORF of the ranked genes.
claims.source: Enrichment in 6mers and 8mers were both detected (only 8mers shown) in the 3'UTRs but not the ORF of the ranked genes (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on Sylamer analysis.

claims.claim: 10 of the 11 downregulated genes identified in the RNA-Seq analysis contained multiple 6mer seed matches for either shL3 and/or shR6.
claims.source: 10 of the 11 downregulated genes identified in the RNA-Seq analysis described in Figure 4A and B contained multiple 6mer seed matches for either shL3 and/or shR6 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The two shRNAs, shL3 and shR6, killed cells by targeting a network of genes enriched in critical survival genes through RNAi.
claims.source: It is therefore likely the two shRNAs, shL3 and shR6, killed cells by targeting a network of genes enriched in critical survival genes through RNAi.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of seed matches in survival genes and the RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: The most abundant mature double-stranded RNAs derived from pLKO-shR6 and pTIP-shL3 were both shifted by one nucleotide from the expected sequence.
claims.source: RNA-Seq analysis performed for the small RNA fraction confirmed in all cases (shScr and shL3 in pTIP, and shScr and shR6 in pLKO), the shRNAs in the cells were cleaved in a way resulting in the predominant formation of an siRNA shifted one nucleotide away from the shRNA loop region (black arrow heads in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by small RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: shRNA-to-siRNA converts of shL3 and shR6 were toxic to HeyA8 cells.
claims.source: These shRNA-to-siRNA converts were toxic to HeyA8 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) confirming that the observed toxicity was not limited to the TRC shRNA platform, but based on a sequence-specific activity of the si/shRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The seed matches of the si/shRNA introduced were significantly enriched in the 3'UTR of downregulated RNAs in cells treated with either shL1 or siL3.
claims.source: In both cases, when the ranked RNA Seq data were subjected to a Sylamer analysis, the seed matches of the si/shRNA introduced were again significantly enriched in the 3'UTR of downregulated RNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Sylamer analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In none of the Sylamer analyses of the four data sets was there enrichment of seed matches in the 3'UTRs of downregulated RNAs that matched the passenger strand.
claims.source: In none of the Sylamer analyses of the four data sets, did we see enrichment of seed matches in the 3'UTRs of downregulated RNAs that matched the passenger strand.
claims.evidence: This is based on Sylamer analysis of all four RNA-Seq data sets.

claims.claim: In all Sylamer analyses, the only significantly enriched sequences matched the seed sequences in the guide strand of the si/shRNAs introduced.
claims.source: In all cases, the only significantly enriched sequences matched the seed sequences in the guide strand of the si/shRNAs we introduced.
claims.evidence: This is based on Sylamer analysis of all four RNA-Seq data sets.

claims.claim: shR7 caused downregulation of 7 of 11 of the same genes targeted by shL3 even though the 6mer seed matches of the two shRNAs are very different.
claims.source: While shL1 did not have much of an effect on the expression of these genes, shR7 caused downregulation of 7 of 11 of the same genes targeted by shL3 even though the 6mer seed matches of the two shRNAs are very different (CTTTGT for shL3 and GGAGGA for shR7) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Survival genes containing a predicted seed match in their 3'UTR were statistically more likely to be downregulated than survival genes without such a motif in most cases.
claims.source: In almost all cases, this analysis revealed that survival genes containing a predicted seed match in their 3'UTR were statistically more likely to be downregulated than survival genes without such a motif.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Fisher's Exact test analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The level of knockdown of the targeted genes and the toxicity of shRNAs were not strictly correlated.
claims.source: Now that we had established that the toxicity of the studied shRNAs involved targeting of survival genes rather than CD95 or CD95L, we had to assume that when studying a larger set of shRNAs that the level of knockdown of the targeted genes and the toxicity were not strictly correlated.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data and confirmed by experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Some toxic shRNAs efficiently silenced CD95 while others did not.
claims.source: While some of the toxic shRNAs efficiently silenced CD95 (i.e. shR6 and shR2) few did not (i.e. shR5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Cells die by DISE due to an early and selective silencing of survival genes through targeting seed matches in their 3'UTR followed by the downregulation of histones.
claims.source: In summary, our analyses suggest that cells die by DISE due to an early and selective silencing of survival genes through targeting seed matches in their 3'UTR followed by the downregulation of histones.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the RNA-Seq and mechanistic data presented.

claims.claim: The pool of 700 shRNAs derived from Venus did not cause any toxicity to NB7 cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, the pool of 700 shRNAs derived from Venus did not cause any toxicity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The pool of shRNAs derived from CD95L ORF significantly slowed down growth of NB7 cells.
claims.source: In contrast, the pool of the shRNAs derived from CD95L significantly slowed down growth, while no toxicity was observed when cells were infected with the pool of shRNAs derived from the CD95L 3'UTR.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: No toxicity was observed when NB7 cells were infected with the pool of shRNAs derived from the CD95L 3'UTR.
claims.source: In contrast, the pool of the shRNAs derived from CD95L significantly slowed down growth, while no toxicity was observed when cells were infected with the pool of shRNAs derived from the CD95L 3'UTR.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Both the shRNAs derived from the CD95 ORF and the 3'UTR showed some toxicity to NB7 cells.
claims.source: In the case of CD95, both the shRNAs derived from the ORF and the 3'UTR showed some toxicity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The shRNAs derived from the CD95 3'UTR caused greater toxicity compared to those derived from the ORF.
claims.source: However, the shRNAs derived from the 3'UTR caused greater toxicity compared to those derived from the ORF.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The shRNAs derived from the CD95L ORF and the CD95 3'UTR contain the most toxic sequences overall.
claims.source: The data suggest that overall the shRNAs derived from the CD95L ORF and the CD95 3'UTR contain the most toxic sequences.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pooled shRNA toxicity data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The highest enrichment of toxic shRNAs was found amongst those with higher TI for the subpool of shRNAs targeting the CD95L ORF followed by shRNAs in the subpool targeting the CD95 3'UTR.
claims.source: Remarkably, the highest enrichment of toxic shRNAs was found amongst those with higher TI for the subpool of shRNAs targeting the CD95L ORF followed by shRNAs in the subpool targeting the CD95 3'UTR.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the toxicity index analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Survival genes contain more seed matches for toxic shRNAs in their 3'UTR than nonsurvival genes regardless of the expression level.
claims.source: This analysis demonstrates survival genes contain more seed matches for toxic shRNAs in their 3'UTR than nonsurvival genes regardless of the expression level.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the alternative TI analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: It is possible to predict the experimental toxicity of shRNAs based on the in silico calculated TI to a certain extent.
claims.source: This suggests, to a certain extent, it is possible to predict the experimental toxicity of shRNAs based on the in silico calculated TI.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between TI and experimental toxicity shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: There was a significant correlation between the GC content of the 6mer seed sequences and higher toxicity of shRNAs detected in the shRNA screen across the CD95L ORF.
claims.source: When the GC content of the 6mer seed sequences of all underrepresented shRNAs detected in the shRNA screen across the CD95L ORF was plotted, we found a significant correlation between the GC content and higher toxicity (indicated by underrepresentation) (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claims.claim: The correlation between GC content and toxicity was even more pronounced when plotting GC content versus the 6mer toxicity index.
claims.source: This correlation was even more pronounced when plotting GC content versus the 6mer toxicity index (Supplementary file 4) (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Higher GC content made shRNAs more toxic, consistent with reports demonstrating that shRNAs with high GC content in the seed region showed decreased on-target and increased off-target activity.
claims.source: While not an absolute requirement, higher GC content made shRNAs more toxic, consistent with reports demonstrating that shRNAs with high GC content in the seed region showed decreased on-target and increased off-target activity (Gu et al., 2014; Ui-Tei et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the correlation data and published literature (Gu et al., 2014; Ui-Tei et al., 2004).

claims.claim: si- and/or shRNAs with certain seed sequences are toxic to cancer cells by targeting critical survival genes through an RNAi mechanism independent of both Drosha and Dicer.
claims.source: In summary, our data suggest that si- and/or shRNAs with certain seed sequences are toxic to cancer cells by targeting critical survival genes through an RNAi mechanism independent of both Drosha and Dicer.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the mechanistic and screening data presented.

claims.claim: High miRNA content, presumably through competing for occupancy in the RISC, might render cells less sensitive to DISE.
claims.source: Furthermore, the data suggest high miRNA content, presumably through competing for occupancy in the RISC, might render cells less sensitive to DISE.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the hypersensitivity of Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells which lack miRNAs.

claims.claim: DISE is a unique form of OTE that results in the simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways in cancer cells.
claims.source: We now demonstrate DISE is a unique form of OTE that results in the simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways in cancer cells.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The discovery that DISE involves loss of multiple survival genes provides an explanation for the unique properties described for this form of cell death, especially the observation that cancer cells have a hard time developing resistance to this cell death mechanism.
claims.source: The discovery that DISE involves loss of multiple survival genes now provides an explanation for the unique properties we described for this form of cell death, especially the observation that cancer cells have a hard time developing resistance to this cell death mechanism (Hadji et al., 2014; Murmann et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the findings and supported by previous publications (Hadji et al., 2014; Murmann et al., 2017).

claims.claim: 98.4% of AGO-associated RNAs in HCT116 cells are miRNAs.
claims.source: Using AGO pull-down experiments, we determined 98.4% of AGO- associated RNAs in HCT116 cells to be miRNAs (99.3% in HeyA8 cells, data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on AGO pull-down experiments.

claims.claim: Drosha-/- cells showed a reduction of miRNA content from roughly 70–80% to 5–6%.
claims.source: It was recently reported that Drosha-/- cells showed a reduction of miRNA content from roughly 70–80% to 5–6%, and Dicer-/- cells showed a reduction down to 14–21% (Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on a published study (Kim et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Dicer-/- cells showed a reduction of miRNA content down to 14–21%.
claims.source: It was recently reported that Drosha-/- cells showed a reduction of miRNA content from roughly 70–80% to 5–6%, and Dicer-/- cells showed a reduction down to 14–21% (Kim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on a published study (Kim et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Neither Drosha-/- nor Dicer-/- cells express reduced AGO2 protein levels.
claims.source: Since neither Drosha-/- nor Dicer-/- cells express reduced AGO2 protein levels (see inset in Figure 3E), it is reasonable to assume that their RISC can take up many more of the toxic DISE inducing RNAs than the RISC in wt cells explaining the super toxicity of both DISE inducing si/shRNAs and CD95L mRNAs in these cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in the inset of Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The RISC in Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells can take up many more of the toxic DISE inducing RNAs than the RISC in wt cells, explaining the super toxicity of both DISE inducing si/shRNAs in these cells.
claims.source: Since neither Drosha-/- nor Dicer-/- cells express reduced AGO2 protein levels (see inset in Figure 3E), it is reasonable to assume that their RISC can take up many more of the toxic DISE inducing RNAs than the RISC in wt cells explaining the super toxicity of both DISE inducing si/shRNAs and CD95L mRNAs in these cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the miRNA depletion and AGO2 expression data.

claims.claim: Expression of either shL3 or shR6 induced DISE in immortalized normal ovarian fibroblasts much more efficiently than in matching nonimmortalized cells.
claims.source: We previously showed expression of either shL3 and shR6 induced DISE in immortalized normal ovarian fibroblasts much more efficiently than in matching nonimmortalized cells (Hadji et al., 2014), suggesting that this form of cell death preferentially affects transformed cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on a previous publication (Hadji et al., 2014).

claims.claim: DISE preferentially affects transformed cells.
claims.source: We previously showed expression of either shL3 and shR6 induced DISE in immortalized normal ovarian fibroblasts much more efficiently than in matching nonimmortalized cells (Hadji et al., 2014), suggesting that this form of cell death preferentially affects transformed cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity of immortalized vs. non-immortalized cells (Hadji et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Cancer cells in general have global downregulation of miRNAs when compared to normal tissues.
claims.source: It is well documented that cancer cells in general have global downregulation of miRNAs when compared to normal tissues (Lu et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on published literature (Lu et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Global downregulation of miRNAs in cancer cells might free up the RISC for DISE-inducing RNAs and would imply that miRNAs may protect normal cells from DISE.
claims.source: This might free up the RISC for DISE-inducing RNAs and would imply that miRNAs may protect normal cells from DISE.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the miRNA downregulation in cancer cells and the hypersensitivity of miRNA-depleted cells to DISE.

claims.claim: Any small RNA with DISE-inducing RNAi activity that does not require Dicer processing can kill cancer cells regardless of Dicer or Drosha status.
claims.source: Overall, our data allow us to predict that any small RNA with DISE-inducing RNAi activity that does not require Dicer processing can kill cancer cells regardless of Dicer or Drosha status.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings with siRNAs in Dicer-/- and Drosha-/- cells.

claims.claim: DISE can be triggered in vivo to treat ovarian cancer in mouse xenografts by delivering CD95L-derived siRNAs using nanoparticles.
claims.source: In fact, in an accompanying manuscript, we demonstrate that DISE can be triggered in vivo to treat ovarian cancer in mouse xenografts by delivering CD95L-derived siRNAs using nanoparticles (Murmann et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is based on an accompanying manuscript (Murmann et al., 2017).

claims.claim: No toxicity was observed in mice treated with CD95L-derived siRNAs using nanoparticles.
claims.source: No toxicity was observed in the treated mice.
claims.evidence: This is based on an accompanying manuscript (Murmann et al., 2017).

claims.claim: It might be possible to develop a novel form of cancer therapy based on the DISE OTE mechanism.
claims.source: These data suggest that it might be possible to develop a novel form of cancer therapy based on the DISE OTE mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the in vivo findings.

results.result: Exogenously added recombinant CD95L protein or overexpressed CD95/CD95L proteins do not protect cells from toxic shRNAs targeting CD95 or CD95L.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 demonstrate through multiple experimental approaches (soluble CD95L treatment, leucine-zipper CD95L, and overexpression of shRNA-resistant CD95/CD95L constructs) that neither exogenous nor overexpressed CD95/CD95L proteins protect cells from shRNA toxicity. The data in Figures 1A, 1D, 1F, and 1G consistently support this conclusion across different cell lines and experimental conditions.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of shRNA/siRNA target sites in CD95 or CD95L genes does not prevent toxicity, demonstrating that cell death is not due to knockdown of these genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 provide strong evidence through CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing experiments (Figures 2A-I) that cells with homozygous deletions of shRNA/siRNA target sites remain fully sensitive to the corresponding toxic RNAs. This definitively establishes that toxicity is not mediated through knockdown of CD95 or CD95L, as stated in C29.

results.result: The toxicity of CD95/CD95L-derived sequences requires canonical RNAi machinery and double-stranded RNA with specific structural features.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C36 demonstrate through systematic structural modifications (Figure 3A-D) that toxicity requires: double-stranded RNA (not single-stranded), ribonucleotides (not DNA), 3' overhangs, and an unmodified 5' end on the guide strand. The competition experiment (C35-C36) further supports RISC involvement. These data collectively establish canonical RNAi mechanism involvement.

results.result: Dicer-/- cells are resistant to toxic shRNAs but sensitive to siRNAs, while Drosha-/- cells are hypersensitive to both, suggesting that cellular miRNAs protect cells from DISE by competing for RISC occupancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C43 present compelling evidence from Dicer-/- and Drosha-/- cells (Figure 3E-G) showing differential sensitivity patterns consistent with the requirement for Dicer processing of shRNAs and the protective role of endogenous miRNAs. The hypersensitivity of both knockout cell types to siRNAs (C42) and the mechanistic explanation involving RISC competition (C43) are well-supported by the data and cited literature.

results.result: The 6mer seed sequence of siL3 is critical for both RNAi activity and toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by the chimeric siRNA experiments shown in Figure 3H, which systematically demonstrate that replacing nucleotides from the seed end abolishes both RNAi activity and toxicity, while replacements from the non-seed end have no effect until the seed region is affected.

results.result: Toxic shRNAs cause early downregulation of 11 genes, including 6 critical survival genes identified in genome-wide screens, with significant enrichment (54.5%, p=3×10⁻⁶) compared to the expected 6.6%.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 are well-supported by the RNA-Seq analysis (Figure 4A-B) using stringent dual-method validation. The statistical enrichment of survival genes (C48) is properly calculated and highly significant. The kinetic analysis (C50) and functional validation (C46-C47) strengthen the conclusion that cells die from silencing multiple survival genes (C51).

results.result: Individual knockdown of seven survival genes reduces cell growth, and a mixture of siRNAs targeting these genes at 1 nM total concentration effectively kills cancer cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by experimental validation (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C) demonstrating that individual and combined knockdown of identified survival genes recapitulates the toxic phenotype. The remarkably low concentration required (35.7 pM per siRNA) is particularly striking and well-documented.

results.result: Survival genes are significantly enriched among downregulated genes in all four RNA-Seq datasets, while nonsurvival genes show no enrichment.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by GSEA analysis (Figure 4D) across all four experimental conditions, providing strong statistical evidence for preferential targeting of survival genes. The consistent pattern across different cell lines, vectors, and timepoints strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: DISE involves substantial downregulation of histones (12 of 16 significantly downregulated genes) and genes involved in mitotic cell cycle, DNA conformation change, and macromolecular complex assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by RNA-Seq data (Figure 4E-F) and Metascape analysis. The argument that histone loss is specific to DISE rather than a general feature of dying cells (C56) is supported by the analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 3, though this interpretation involves some inference.

results.result: Sylamer analysis identifies strong enrichment of cognate seed matches in 3'UTRs (but not ORFs) of downregulated genes, and 10 of 11 downregulated genes contain multiple seed matches for shL3 and/or shR6.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are well-supported by Sylamer analysis (Figure 5A) and seed match mapping (Figure 5B). The statistical significance of enrichment and the specificity for 3'UTRs (C59) provide strong evidence for canonical RNAi-mediated targeting of survival genes through their 3'UTRs.

results.result: Small RNA-Seq reveals that mature shRNAs are predominantly cleaved one nucleotide away from the expected position, and synthetic siRNAs based on these sequences are toxic.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by small RNA-Seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and functional validation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B). This finding explains the discrepancy between expected and observed seed sequences in Sylamer analysis and confirms sequence-specific toxicity independent of the shRNA platform.

results.result: Sylamer analysis of shL1 and siL3 treatments confirms enrichment of guide strand seed matches in 3'UTRs of downregulated genes, with no enrichment of passenger strand sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 extend the Sylamer findings to additional experimental conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), demonstrating the generality of the mechanism. The absence of passenger strand enrichment (C65-C66) confirms that toxicity is mediated specifically by the guide strand.

results.result: Different toxic shRNAs with distinct seed sequences can target overlapping sets of survival genes, and survival genes with predicted seed matches are statistically more likely to be downregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and Fisher's Exact test analysis (Figure 5C). The finding that shR7 targets 7 of 11 genes also targeted by shL3 despite different seed sequences (C67) suggests convergent targeting of survival gene networks.

results.result: The level of on-target knockdown and toxicity of shRNAs are not strictly correlated, with some toxic shRNAs efficiently silencing CD95 while others do not.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3, demonstrating that toxicity is not simply a function of on-target knockdown efficiency. This finding is important for understanding that DISE operates through off-target effects rather than on-target gene silencing.

results.result: DISE involves early selective silencing of survival genes through 3'UTR targeting followed by histone downregulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is a well-supported summary inference integrating the RNA-Seq data, Sylamer analysis, kinetic studies, and mechanistic experiments. The temporal sequence (early survival gene silencing followed by histone loss) is supported by the kinetic data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

results.result: A screen of 4666 shRNAs reveals that toxic sequences are enriched in the CD95L ORF and CD95 3'UTR, with the Venus control showing no toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C72-C77 are supported by the pooled shRNA toxicity experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). The differential toxicity patterns across different gene regions provide important insights into the distribution of DISE-inducing sequences. However, the mechanistic basis for this regional enrichment is not fully explained.

results.result: The Toxicity Index (TI), based on the ratio of seed matches in survival vs. nonsurvival gene 3'UTRs, correlates with experimental toxicity and can predict shRNA toxicity to some extent.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by the TI analysis (Figure 7B) and validation with expression-matched genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The statistical significance of enrichment and the correlation between predicted and observed toxicity support the utility of TI as a predictive tool, though the authors appropriately note limitations ('to a certain extent').

results.result: Higher GC content in 6mer seed sequences correlates significantly with increased shRNA toxicity, consistent with reports of decreased on-target and increased off-target activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 7C-E) and are consistent with published literature. However, the authors appropriately note that high GC content is not an absolute requirement for toxicity, and the mechanistic basis for this correlation could be more thoroughly explored.

results.result: si/shRNAs with certain seed sequences kill cancer cells by targeting survival genes through RNAi independent of Drosha and Dicer, and high miRNA content may protect cells by competing for RISC occupancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 represent well-supported summary conclusions integrating the mechanistic studies with Dicer-/- and Drosha-/- cells, the RNA-Seq data, and the Sylamer analysis. The independence from Drosha/Dicer for siRNAs (but not shRNAs) is clearly demonstrated, and the protective role of miRNAs is a reasonable inference from the hypersensitivity data.

results.result: DISE is a unique form of off-target effect where >80% of CD95/CD95L-targeting si/shRNAs kill cancer cells through canonical RNAi by targeting 3'UTRs of multiple survival genes, explaining the simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways and resistance to resistance development.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C86-C87 represent the central thesis of the paper. The >80% figure (C1) is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and published data. The mechanism involving canonical RNAi and survival gene targeting (C2) is extensively validated throughout the manuscript. The explanation for unique DISE properties (C87) is a reasonable inference supported by the data and cited literature.

results.result: Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells are hypersensitive to DISE, suggesting that cellular miRNAs protect cells from this form of cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 are well-supported by the experimental data in Figure 3E and 3G with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.0001). The inference that miRNAs protect cells (C4) is reasonable given the miRNA depletion in these cells and the competition model for RISC occupancy.

results.result: Specific toxic RNAi-active sequences present in the genome can kill cancer cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is a proposal/conclusion based on the collective findings, particularly the shRNA screen identifying toxic sequences in CD95L ORF. While labeled as 'SPECULATION' in evidence type, this is actually a well-supported conclusion from the extensive experimental data, though it represents a conceptual synthesis rather than a directly tested hypothesis.

results.result: DsiRNAs targeting CD95L are toxic at 5 nM, and analysis of published genome-wide data shows that 67% of CD95/CD95L-targeting shRNAs killed >50% of 216 tested cancer cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C12 are supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and reanalysis of published datasets (Cowley et al., 2014). The consistency between the authors' findings and independent large-scale screens strengthens the generality of the DISE phenomenon.

results.result: miR-30-based shRNAs show reduced toxicity and knockdown efficiency compared to pLKO/pTIP-based shRNAs, likely due to insufficient expression levels, while siL3 is toxic at concentrations as low as 1 nM.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 are supported by comparative experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-E) explaining the discrepancy with published screens using miR-30 platforms. The dose-response data for siL3 (C18) establishes that DISE can occur at very low concentrations when expression is sufficient.

results.result: 98.4% of AGO-associated RNAs are miRNAs in wild-type cells, while Drosha-/- and Dicer-/- cells show dramatic miRNA depletion but maintain AGO2 expression, allowing increased uptake of toxic RNAs into RISC.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 integrate the authors' AGO pull-down data with published findings (Kim et al., 2016) to provide a mechanistic explanation for the hypersensitivity of miRNA-depleted cells. The inference about increased RISC availability (C92) is reasonable given the maintained AGO2 levels and depleted miRNA content.

results.result: DISE preferentially affects transformed cells over normal cells, potentially explained by global miRNA downregulation in cancer cells freeing up RISC for DISE-inducing RNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 combine previous findings (Hadji et al., 2014) with established knowledge about miRNA downregulation in cancer (Lu et al., 2005) to propose a mechanism for cancer cell selectivity. While the model is reasonable and consistent with the data, direct experimental validation of this specific mechanism in normal vs. cancer cells would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: DISE can be triggered in vivo to treat ovarian cancer without toxicity, suggesting potential for developing a novel cancer therapy based on this mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are based on an accompanying manuscript (Murmann et al., 2017) demonstrating in vivo efficacy and safety. While the therapeutic potential (C100) is appropriately presented as speculative ('might be possible'), the in vivo proof-of-concept provides strong support for this possibility.
